cards.front: Why does a dead body's core temperature fall after death?
cards.back: Heat production from **respiration** stops, but heat is still lost to the surroundings, so the body cools until it matches the **ambient temperature**.
cards.hint: Think about where a living body's heat comes from and what happens when that supply stops.

cards.front: Why do muscles stiffen after death?
cards.back: Respiration stops, so no new **ATP** is made. Without ATP, myosin heads cannot detach from actin, so the muscles stay locked and stiff.
cards.hint: Think about what happens to the energy supply once respiration stops.

cards.front: Why is combining several methods more reliable than using just one to estimate time of death?
cards.back: No single method is precise. Where estimates from temperature, rigor mortis, decomposition and insects overlap, confidence in the time of death is higher.
cards.hint: Consider which method is most useful at different times after death.

cards.back: The study of **insects** and their life cycles to provide evidence in legal investigations, such as estimating time of death.
cards.hint: Think about what decaying bodies attract.

cards.front: Which equation gives the average rate of fall in body temperature?
cards.back: $\text{rate} = \frac{\text{fall in temperature}}{\text{time}}$, giving $^{\circ}\mathrm{C\,h^{-1}}$ when time is in hours.

cards.front: A body cools from 37.0 °C to 31.0 °C in 5.0 hours. What is its average rate of fall?
cards.hint: Work out the fall in temperature first.

cards.front: A student says rigor mortis happens because the muscles dry out. Why is this wrong?
cards.back: Rigor mortis is caused by the loss of ATP supply, which stops myosin heads detaching from actin. Drying out is not the explanation and earns no marks.

cards.front: How does rigor mortis change over time after death?
cards.back: Stiffening starts within a few hours, often in the face and jaw, spreads, and is generally complete after about half a day. Later the muscle proteins break down and the body becomes flexible again.
cards.hint: Think about the order of events and how temperature affects the speed.

cards.back: The breakdown of dead tissue by **saprobionts** and enzymes.
cards.hint: Consider which organisms feed on dead material.

cards.front: Name three factors that change how fast a body decomposes.
cards.back: Temperature, oxygen and moisture. Access by insects and the body itself, such as its size, clothing and open wounds, also matter.
cards.hint: Think about both the environment and the body.

cards.front: Why can decay alone not give an exact time since death?
cards.back: Decomposition does not follow a fixed timetable. The same body decays at very different rates in warm and cold settings, so it gives only a rough estimate.

cards.front: Why can blowfly life cycles be used to estimate time since death?
cards.back: Each stage lasts a known time, longer in cool conditions and shorter in warm ones, so the stages present on a body act as a clock.
cards.hint: Think about how the length of each stage changes with temperature.

cards.front: Eggs take 1 day, larvae 6 days, and the oldest pupae have been pupating 2 days. How long ago were the eggs laid?
cards.back: About $9$ days, because $1+6+2=9$, so death happened at least 9 days ago.
cards.hint: Add the time spent in each stage.

cards.front: Why does insect evidence give only a minimum time since death?
cards.back: Flies may reach the body some time after death, so the insects only show how long the eggs have been there. Death was at least that long ago.
cards.hint: Think about when the first flies could reach the body.
